segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees gathered around him, along with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they saw that some of his disciples were eating their bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they wash themselves. And there are many other things that they have received to hold to: the washing of cups and pitchers and copper vessels and dining couches.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with defiled hands?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In vain they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your own tradition!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must surely die.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you say that if a person tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever benefit you might have had from me is Corban’

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: — that is, an offering —

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down. And you do many things like that.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Calling the crowd to him again, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nothing that goes into a person from outside is able to defile them; rather, the things that come out of a person are what defile the person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had gone into a house, away from the crowd, his disciples asked him about the parable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So you too are without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: because it goes not into the heart but into the stomach, and goes out into the latrine?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In saying this, he declared all foods clean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went on,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles the person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For from within, out of the human heart, come evil designs: sexual immorality, thefts, murders,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: adulteries, acts of greed and wickedness, deceit, debauchery, an envious eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All these wicked things come from within and defile the person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not escape notice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell at his feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let the children first eat their fill, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because of what you have said, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went away to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he left the region of Tyre again and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the middle of the region of the Decapolis.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking him aside from the crowd, in private, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched his tongue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ephphatha,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is, “Be opened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak clearly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, all the more they kept proclaiming it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astonished beyond all measure, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “He has done everything well; he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”

notes.note: The Greek word is literally 'common', used in Jewish Greek for what is ordinary and so not ritually pure. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene. Mark's gloss 'that is, unwashed' and the explanation in verses 3 and 4 suggest he expected readers unfamiliar with Jewish practice.

The Greek says literally 'with a fist', and what that meant is not known. Proposals include washing with a cupped hand, with a fistful of water, up to the wrist, or by rubbing the fist in the other palm. Many translations paraphrase with 'carefully' or 'ceremonially', and some manuscripts read 'often' instead. The literal wording is kept because none of the explanations is certain.

The verb is the one elsewhere rendered 'baptize', and the related noun stands behind 'washing' later in the verse. Here both refer to Jewish ritual washing, possibly by immersion. The clause may also mean that they do not eat anything from the marketplace unless they wash it. Some early manuscripts read 'sprinkle' instead.
Several important early manuscripts lack these words. SBLGNT includes them, and they are translated here. The Greek word can mean a bed or a couch for reclining at meals.

Corban is a Hebrew term for something dedicated to God as an offering, which Mark translates for his readers. Declaring property Corban was a vow that put it beyond another person's use. Jesus's charge is that the vow was upheld even when it deprived parents of the support owed them under the commandment to honor them. The details of how such vows worked in this period are only partly known.

Verse 16 ('If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear') is absent from important early manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. Most scholars regard it as a later addition modelled on similar sayings elsewhere in Mark.

notes.phrase: In saying this, he declared all foods clean.
notes.note: The Greek is a participle, literally 'cleansing all foods'. In the earliest manuscripts its form is masculine and is most naturally read as the narrator's comment on what Jesus's words imply, which is the view of most modern scholars and translations. Later manuscripts have a neuter form that makes the phrase part of Jesus's sentence, describing digestion, as in the King James Version.

The Greek is literally 'an evil eye'. In Jewish idiom this meant a grudging, envious or stingy attitude toward others, not the curse-casting glance the English phrase now suggests. Many modern translations simply put 'envy'; this rendering keeps the eye of the idiom while giving its sense.

'Greek' here marks the woman as a non-Jew of Greek language and culture, not as a native of Greece; some translations put 'a Gentile'. 'Syrophoenician' places her origin in Phoenicia, the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, which belonged to the Roman province of Syria.

The Greek word is a diminutive of 'dog'. Some scholars take it to mean household dogs or puppies, which suits the picture of dogs under the table and softens the saying. Others point out that diminutives had often lost their force in Koine, and that Mark uses many, and so render simply 'dogs'. Either way the saying puts the 'children', Israel, ahead of Gentiles, and the woman accepts the image and turns it to her advantage.

The Greek address can be an ordinary polite 'sir' or the title 'Lord'. On the lips of a Gentile stranger the polite sense is the more likely, though Mark's Christian readers may well have heard more in it. Some manuscripts read 'Yes, Lord'.

notes.traditional: had an impediment in his speech
notes.note: The Greek word is very rare. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Isaiah 35:6, in a passage promising that the ears of the deaf will be opened and the tongue of those who can hardly speak will be made clear. Mark's choice of word, together with the crowd's words in verse 37, probably points the reader to that promise.
Mark preserves the word in Jesus's own language and then translates it, as he does with a few other sayings. It is usually identified as Aramaic, though some have argued it is Hebrew.
